newsitem.title: USA: USDA eases CRP rules, new signup later this year.
newsitem.headline: USDA eases CRP rules, new signup later this year.

text.p: Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman removed an obstacle Wednesday for farmers who need to prepare CRP land for planting and said a new signup will be offered later this year for the Conservation Reserve Program.

The steps announced by Glickman responded to a request from 14 farm-state senators to help farmers who had to begin field preparation while waiting to see if their land would be accepted for the reserve.
Senate Agriculture Committee chairman Richard Lugar, Indiana Republican, said Glickman's decision "will be very helpful to winter crop producers whose CRP contracts are expiring this fall."
In his letter, Glickman renewed his pledge that farmers would be told by late May if their bids were accepted.

"For farmers in arid areas whose CRP contracts expire September 30, 1997, and who intend to plant a fall-seeded crop, USDA will not reduce their CRP rental payments if they have destroyed or will destroy vegetative crop cover on their expiring CRP land on or after May 1," Glickman wrote.

USDA will offer farmers another chance to enroll in CRP "this calendar year and will announce which offers it will accept in a timely manner so that farmers who grow fall-seeded crops will be able to begin preparing their land next spring for planting fall crops for harvest in 1999," Glickman said.

A Lugar aide said earlier in the day that the letter written by the senators "outlines an agreement...to solve the CRP fall-planting issue." It would end a potential legislative showdown over a House-passed bill to allow unilateral extension of CRP contracts by farmers with fall-planted crops.
Several million acres, mostly winter wheat, could be involved in the dispute.

Contracts on 21 million acres of CRP land expire this fall. Farmers offered 25.6 million acres during a month-long signup in March. USDA has said it might accept up to 19 million acres. Maximum CRP enrollment is 36.4 million acres.
